location.value: West-central Africa: from the Atlantic coast to the Kwango River, and from the Congo River to the Kwanza. Today northern Angola and parts of the two Congos.

terrain.value: Plateau and river valleys near the Congo estuary.
terrain.source: Thornton, A History of West Central Africa to 1850 (2020)

resources.value: Farmland, raffia cloth, copper, salt, and nzimbu shells from Luanda Island.

disasters.value: Not specifically documented in the sources checked.

population.value: About 780,000–790,000 people in 1623 (Wikipedia gives both figures).

urbanisation.value: The capital M’banza-Kongo (São Salvador) had about 100,000 people by the early 1600s, partly from relocated captives.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Captives were moved to the capital. Very many people were sold into the Atlantic slave trade.

economicBase.value: Farming, crafts (raffia cloth), and tribute. The king deliberately concentrated people around the capital.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with Portugal from 1483. The Atlantic slave trade grew, and King Afonso I protested its abuses to Portugal in 1526.

moneyAndTax.value: Nzimbu shells (a royal monopoly), and lubongo and mpusu cloth as currency. Tribute from provinces.

inequality.value: A royal elite and nobles above free villagers and slaves. Enslavement of subjects increased in the 17th century.

governmentType.value: An elective monarchy: kings were chosen by a council of electors, with provinces under appointed governors.

keyRulers.value: Lukeni lua Nimi (founder, c. 1390). Nzinga a Nkuwu (baptised João I, 1491). Afonso I (1509–1542). Garcia II. António I (killed at Mbwila, 1665). Pedro IV (reunified 1709).

succession.value: Elective among royal descendants, which led to factional rivalry (the Kinlaza and Kimpanzu houses).

institutions.value: A royal council, provincial governors, and a Catholic Church organisation (a diocese recognised by Rome in 1596).

stability.value: Stable until the 1660s. Then the Kongo Civil War (1665–1709) after the defeat at Mbwila. São Salvador was sacked in 1678.

eliteConflict.value: Rival royal houses fighting for the throne during the civil war.

armyAndTech.value: Archers and heavy infantry, adding musketeers from the 1580s.

majorWars.value: Wars with Portuguese Angola: Mbanda Kasi (1623) and the Battle of Mbwila (1665), where King António I was killed.

territoryChange.value: About 129,400 km² in 1623 (Wikipedia infobox). It lost power after 1665 and became a Portuguese vassal (1857/1862).

alliancesRivals.value: Ally and trade partner of Portugal, later its enemy and then its vassal. Briefly allied with the Dutch (1640s). Rivals: Ndongo and Portuguese Angola.

inventions.value: Fine raffia textiles, and metalworking (iron and copper).
inventions.source: Thornton, A History of West Central Africa to 1850 (2020)

scienceEducation.value: Literacy in Portuguese among the elite after 1491. Kongolese nobles studied in Portugal.

openness.value: Very open: it adopted Christianity and Portuguese titles and writing, and exchanged embassies with Portugal and Rome.

religion.value: Roman Catholicism became the state religion after 1491, blended with local beliefs. The Antonian movement (1704–1708, led by Beatriz Kimpa Vita).

languageWriting.value: Kikongo, plus Portuguese and Latin for writing and church use.

artsArchitecture.value: Stone churches at M’banza-Kongo (from 1491), crucifixes, and raffia textiles.

socialStructure.value: Royal family and nobles, free villagers, and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Kongolese Christian identity and loyalty to the Mwene Kongo (king).
sharedIdentity.source: Thornton, A History of West Central Africa to 1850 (2020)

neighbours.value: Ndongo, Matamba, Loango, Portuguese Angola, and the Dutch.

ideasReligions.value: One of the first sub-Saharan kingdoms to adopt Christianity, and an early African partner of European diplomacy.

colonisation.value: Colonised. It became a Portuguese vassal in the 19th century. Portugal abolished the monarchy in 1914 after a revolt, and the territory was split between Portuguese Angola and the Belgian Congo.

riseSignals.value: Founded around 1390 through conquest and political marriage, then centralised royal power.

peakPeriod.value: The 16th to early 17th century (Afonso I to the 1620s).

declineSignals.value: The Atlantic slave trade, wars with Portuguese Angola, the defeat at Mbwila (1665), and civil war.

outcome.value: Reunified in 1709 but weakened. It became a Portuguese vassal and was abolished in 1914. The royal title continued as an honour until 1975.

sources.value: Kongolese royal letters (in Portuguese), missionary accounts, and Portuguese records. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026 (later sections only summarised). See also Thornton (2020).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. The founding date and early rulers rely on tradition. Vassalage is dated 1857 or 1862, and population is given as 780,000 or 790,000 for 1623.
